title: Caesar's coin (Mark 12:13–17)
hook: whose image is on it? give Caesar his, and God what is God's

segments.voice: Yesterday, the vineyard tenants, and your line was the rejected stone. Who did you notice that others overlook? Day two hundred eleven.

Next come some Pharisees together with some Herodians, supporters of Herod's family, which ruled with Rome's blessing. Normally these two groups didn't agree on much. Mark says they were sent to catch him in his words. They start with flattery, thick as honey. Teacher, we know you're honest, you don't care what anyone thinks, you teach God's way truly. And then the question: is it lawful to pay the tax to Caesar, or not? Should we pay, or shouldn't we? It's the perfect trap. Say yes, and the crowd, who hate the Roman tax, will see a collaborator. Say no, and the Herodians have a rebel to report to Rome. There's no safe answer. So Jesus asks for something small.
screen: `AN ODD PAIR, SENT TO CATCH HIM.` → `FLATTERY, THICK AS HONEY.` → `SHALL WE GIVE, OR NOT?`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible, he says: "bring me a penny, that I may see it." The penny was a denarius, a silver coin, about a day's wage. And notice: he has to ask for one. He doesn't carry it. They do, right there in the temple courts. Then the question: "Whose is this image and superscription?" Image and inscription. And they answer: "Caesar's." The coins of that emperor, Tiberius, carried his face, and many carried words calling him the son of the divine Augustus. Then the line: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." And Mark says they marveled at him. Here's what's hiding in it. The word for image is the same idea as the first chapter of the Bible, where God makes human beings in his own image. So if a coin with Caesar's face on it belongs to Caesar, give it back to him. But what has God's image stamped on it? You do. Every person does. Caesar can have the coin. God asks for the person. Christians have drawn many practical conclusions from this line. Some hear a clear line between church and state. Others hear a limit on what any government can claim. Many Christians pay their taxes and also say that conscience belongs to God alone. What they share is the picture: a face on a coin, and a face in the mirror, and the question of whose each one is.
screen: `BRING ME A PENNY.` · `WHOSE IMAGE IS THIS?` · `GIVE CAESAR WHAT BEARS HIS FACE.` · `YOU BEAR GOD'S IMAGE.` · then, large: `RENDER TO CAESAR THE THINGS THAT ARE CAESAR'S, AND TO GOD THE THINGS THAT ARE GOD'S.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask whose image you bear. Settle, and breathe. If you have a coin or a bill nearby, hold it and look at the face on it. If not, picture one. Then think about your own face, the one you'll see in the mirror tonight. The Bible says it carries God's image. Let that sit for a minute. What in your day belongs to Caesar, to the bills and the job and the rules? And what belongs only to God? If you pray, you can offer that part back. The bell holds the time.
Caesar's coin. A denarius with the emperor's face: give it to Caesar, and give to God what bears God's image.
Your line: you bear god's image. Today, when you see someone's face, remember whose image it carries, and treat them that way. Day two hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Christians often quote "render to Caesar" in discussions of faith, taxes and government, and many teach from Genesis 1:27 that every person bears God's image and so deserves dignity.

fork.setup: you're asked in front of a crowd: should we pay the tax to Caesar, or not? yes makes you a collaborator; no makes you a rebel. what do you do?
options: ask for a coin, and ask whose image is on it.
fork.reveal: he asks for a penny: "Whose is this image and superscription?" then: give Caesar what is Caesar's, and God what is God's. and they marveled.

original.note: Greek: image, likeness. the root of the English icon. the same word the Greek Bible uses in Genesis 1:27.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus says pay your taxes.
what it means: the coin bears Caesar's image, so give it back; you bear God's image, so give yourself to God.
what a scholar hears: eikōn, as in the Greek of Genesis 1:27, and a denarius of Tiberius calling him son of the divine Augustus.

notes: The denarius of Tiberius (inscription TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS) is the usual identification; Mark doesn't name the emperor. Confirm 'many carried words calling him the son of the divine Augustus'.
Genesis 1:27 in the Septuagint uses eikōn; confirm.
Herodians described as 'supporters of Herod's family, which ruled with Rome's blessing'; confirm.
Three church-and-state readings kept general and unranked.
